newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Confidence wanes in quick Taleban victory.
newsitem.headline: Confidence wanes in quick Taleban victory.

text.p: Confidence is waning in the Afghan capital Kabul that the purist Islamic Taleban will be able to gain a quick victory over opposing forces.

The defection on Monday to the Taleban of a senior opposition commander, General Abdul Malik, raised hopes that their opponents were on the verge of defeat and that Afghanistan would be under one government for the first time in almost 20 years.

News of Malik's defection sent the value of the Afghani, the country's currency, up by 30 per cent, from 24,300 to the dollar to 16,000. The Afghani's value is one of the more sensitive barometers of public confidence.
"The developments looked at first as if the Taleban would take over the whole of the north in one month so the Afghani strengthened," money dealer Ghafour Ahmad told Reuters on Thursday.
"With the capture of the north by the Taleban, people think that war will end and the country will be at peace." he added.
However, doubts began surfacing soon after Malik's move about the real extent of the Taleban gains.
The Taleban said they had taken two provinces.

But their opponents -- an alliance grouping General Abdul Rashid Dostum with Shi'ite leader Karim Khalili and ousted President Burhanuddin Rabbani's commander Ahmad Shah Masood -- claimed they were keeping the Taleban out of their territory.
With the opposing forces falling back and establishing a new front-line to the east of the rebel province, there were fears the war might resettle into another period of stalemate.
Malik's defection, in a revolt against Dostum, ended 18 months of stand-off on the front-line in northwestern Afghanistan, where neither side was able to make significant gains.
In Kabul's money market on Thursday the price of the Afghani started to slide against the dollar, reaching 19,200 in the afternoon.

The war in Afghanistan has destroyed the backbone of Afghanistan's economy -- trade. With few easily exploitable natural resources, the country has always made its money from being a crossroads between between east and west.

With the communist invasion in 1979 and the descent into chaos that occured after the communist defeat in 1992, trade has been reduced to a trickle. The export of narcotics now ranks as Afghanistan's number one foreign exchange earner.
Afghans hope that, whatever the politics of the Taleban, they will be able to reopen trade routes, particularly between Central Asia and the subcontinent.
The Afghans are not the only ones waiting, and hoping, for peace.

Two oil companies, Unocal of the United States and Bridas of Argentina, are already competing to build a $2.5-billion gas pipeline from energy-rich Turkmenistan in the north, to Pakistan in the south. What the future holds is very much on their minds.
